ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Metabolic pathology covers inherited and acquired disorders of energy production and storage. Clinicians diagnose by linking biochemical derangements to clinical syndromes, then treat the underlying defect and support organ function.

sections.p: Metabolic disorders arise when enzymes, transporters or regulatory pathways fail, leading to accumulation or deficiency of key metabolites. They can be inherited or acquired, and often present with multisystem signs.
b: Inherited defects are usually autosomal recessive; acquired causes include infections, toxins, and nutritional deficiencies.

sections.p: Normal metabolism relies on tightly regulated enzymatic cascades. Each step is controlled by feedback, co‑factor availability, and gene expression. Disruption at any point alters substrate levels and downstream products.
b: Enzyme deficiency → substrate build‑up, product loss; transporter defect → impaired uptake or excretion; regulatory failure → inappropriate enzyme activity.

sections.p: Metabolic pathways are controlled by allosteric effectors, covalent modifications, and transcriptional control. Hormones (insulin, glucagon) and cellular energy status (ATP/AMP) modulate key enzymes.
b: Hexokinase vs glucokinase in glucose phosphorylation; pyruvate dehydrogenase complex regulated by pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase.

sections.p: Common mechanisms: enzyme deficiency, co‑factor deficiency, transporter malfunction, mitochondrial dysfunction, and hormonal dysregulation. Clinical severity depends on residual activity and metabolic load.

t.b: Elevated lactate indicates impaired oxidative phosphorylation; high levels predict organ failure.
Hyperammonemia suggests urea cycle defect or hepatic failure; rapid rise is life‑threatening.
Presence in urine indicates impaired glucose utilization or fatty acid oxidation.
Impaired response suggests insulin resistance or beta‑cell dysfunction.

sections.p: Metabolic disorders manifest with nonspecific symptoms—vomiting, lethargy, failure to thrive—making early recognition critical. Prompt diagnosis prevents irreversible organ damage.

t.b: Hypoglycemia (<2.5 mmol/L) requires immediate dextrose; hyperglycemia (>10 mmol/L) indicates diabetes.
Positive ketones in a non‑diabetic patient suggest starvation or fatty acid oxidation defect.

sections.p: Remember the classic triad of metabolic acidosis: low pH, low bicarbonate, and elevated anion gap. Use the anion gap to differentiate causes (lactate, ketoacids, toxins).
b: Anion gap = Na+ – (Cl– + HCO3–). Normal 8–12 mEq/L.
High gap → lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, renal failure, toxins.

sections.p: Treat the precipitating factor, correct metabolic derangements, and address the underlying defect. Supportive care includes fluid, electrolytes, and organ monitoring.

t.b: Corrects hypoglycemia; avoid if hyperglycemia present.
Reduces ammonia absorption in urea cycle disorders.

sections.p: Many metabolic disorders mimic endocrine or infectious diseases. For example, lactic acidosis can resemble sepsis; hypoglycemia can be mistaken for adrenal insufficiency.
b: Lactic acidosis vs sepsis: lactate >5 mmol/L with normal WBC may suggest mitochondrial failure.

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal early in disease or due to sample handling. For instance, ammonia can be low if the sample is delayed.
b: Check sample timing; repeat if clinical suspicion remains high.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypoglycemia, hyperammonemia, unexplained seizures, sudden cardiac arrhythmia in a patient with known metabolic disorder

faq.q: How do I differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes in a child?
faq.a: Type 1 shows ketoacidosis, low C‑peptide, and autoantibodies; type 2 has higher C‑peptide, insulin resistance signs, and often obesity.

faq.q: What is the first step in managing hyperammonemia?
faq.a: Immediate ammonia reduction with lactulose or dialysis, followed by protein restriction and nitrogen scavengers.

faq.q: Can a low‑protein diet cure phenylketonuria?
faq.a: It prevents neurotoxicity but does not cure the enzyme deficiency; lifelong dietary management is required.

exam: Explain the biochemical basis of the anion gap and its clinical utility.
Describe the diagnostic workup for a child with unexplained hypoglycemia.
Outline the management of a patient with acute hyperammonemia due to a urea cycle defect.
